note: Conversations the artist had about the work, oldest first, plus collaborators. Each entry paraphrases the other person; the artist's replies are left out, except a short note on what changed or, where asked, the answer in progress.

entries.role: speculative architect and director, the artist's first teacher at SCI-Arc
entries.said: The first conversation. Think of the Tamagotchi, the small Japanese digital pet that lives only as long as it is fed, a little at a time. A creature can be digital and still feel alive to the person who feeds it. He pointed to artists who stage digital creatures, among them an exhibition called Beings, where soft bodies walk forward together like a herd of imagined animals.
entries.led_to: From there the artist followed Lenia, a smooth Game of Life, into artificial life, and later showed the work at the ALIFE 2026 workshop and art gallery.

entries.role: the artist's advisor, MIT Media Lab
entries.said: Read the project early on as speculative design. The topics it touches and the questions it asks are worth discussing. Look at how other organisms in the living world make their next generation, and keep gathering examples.

entries.role: chair, ACM SIGGRAPH Digital Arts Committee
entries.said: Look at the Chinese word for life, 生命. 生 is birth and being alive; 命 is the state, the rules and the conditions that keep a life going. Even 机器 (machine) and 机器人 (machine with the character for person) differ a little. Together they found the phrase robotic womb for the subtitle and defined it in simple words.

entries.who: An artist with a background in marine biology
entries.role: shown in the SIGGRAPH 2026 Art Gallery with two talking robots worn on the shoulders
entries.said: Some sea creatures have no fixed sex. She was the first to raise this, and it opened the question of whether a mother is a sex, a gender or a role.

entries.who: A visitor met at Ars Electronica
entries.said: The question is interesting, but approach it with caution.
The digital part and the physical part are only loosely tied. The simulation and the robot need a stronger technical link between them. He sent an example of how such a link can work.

As it stands the work is neither artistic enough nor hard core enough as engineering. And once the baby is born with no arm, how could the baby bear a next generation? Without an arm the baby cannot reproduce.
entries.led_to: The arm and the printed shell became separate parts, so a born baby can be fitted with an arm by assembly and bear the next one.

entries.who: An instructor of the City Science class
entries.said: Born, Not Made is a good name; there may be an even better one, but do not change it until a better one appears. The cord between mother and child is like the tie between the mother robot and the arm.

themes: a body, not only a simulation
entries.said: In a first conversation: the work is directly related to artificial life; reach out to Melanie Mitchell at the Santa Fe Institute. Then the question a thesis defense will ask: why does the work need a physical body? Why is a simulation not enough?
entries.answer: Touch is one answer: a body reaches past the screen and answers the hand directly. The other: only a body shares our time and space. In the physical world the robot stands where other animals stand, as one species among others, close to equal.

entries.said: Not a warning to be careful with AI, but a reminder to be aware of the problem. Being aware is what matters, and that is enough.

entries.who: A researcher in the Personal Robots group
entries.said: Why was Jibo so loved? Its small shifts of expression and motion feel so natural that people forget how hard they were to make. Interaction with a robot works when it is smooth enough to go unnoticed.

entries.who: An MIT graduate of more than 30 years ago
entries.role: met at the World in Action hackathon, Los Angeles
entries.said: Many people are afraid of AI. A small, lovable robot body changes that. A robot mother raising a baby shows AI as gentle, even lovable, and then people may stop being afraid.
The first to point to cyberfeminism as a reading of the work. Also asked why a male artist is drawn to this question.

entries.who: A friend in the MIT MDes program
entries.said: The idea is sexy.
Do you really understand what birth is? Birth may be too big a word, and using it for AI or a robot may be a misuse of it.
The work needs a trunk, one line that everything else hangs from. Artificial life is close enough to the project to be that trunk.

entries.who: A robotics PhD student at Stanford
entries.role: founded a company and ran it for years before returning to Stanford for a PhD
entries.said: Robots today fold laundry, sew clothes and do small chores, and that work has worn away the love people once had for robots. As children we loved giant heroes like Ultraman, figures with a philosophy and a meaning behind them. Even as an art project, this work has that kind of vision.
Why not call it parent and baby rather than mother and baby? Is the work a small model of human society? Can the baby have a next generation of the baby's own? And is there a father?

entries.who: A senior researcher based in New York
entries.said: Touch is the point to hold on to. Between people, and above all between a mother and a child, touch is the first bond. If the tank were very large, with one robot bearing the next and that one bearing the next, many interesting things could emerge. At the end of the talk she said she is a mother too, and asked for a hug.

entries.role: Responsive Environments, MIT Media Lab; independent study advisor
contributed: The way the baby is born: the arm pushes while the baby inflates.
Floating: made large enough, the body is carried by the water, since water can bear a great deal of weight.
Touch sensing by capacitance, so a hand on the robot is felt: a very simple principle that works.
entries.said: Kept asking why the work is made this way, and what kind of interaction would feel natural. Many ways of interacting were tried before settling on the plainest one: touch the body directly. A hand on the mother feels the pump drawing water little by little, a faint pulse, as if the body were alive. Touch cannot be replaced.

contributed: One of the first to hear the idea and find it worth pursuing.
Much of the writing work around the project.
entries.said: Explored what kind of group the robots form and what state the group is in. As a large installation, one robot bears the next and that one bears the next, and the relations between them become the work.

entries.role: PhD candidate in Computer Science, Northwestern University
contributed: Proposed printing in a liquid gel bath, drawing on a paper he coauthored that prints epoxy in a Carbopol bath (EpoMemory, CHI 2023).
Proposed replacing the 3D printer axes with a robot arm.
entries.said: Willing to propose bold changes of direction. When the team was leaning toward an automatic printing rig, he asked whether a liquid would be better, and later whether an arm could replace the printer axes, which were hard to take apart, looked too much like a machine and could do only one thing.

contributed: Proposed an early printing rig that the team used for a while.
Travelled to Changzhou, China, to visit factories and examine a robot arm made to be built into other machines, close to the project's own idea of an arm inside a body.
